report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

info.title: Young Children's Resistance to Immoral Actions 1 "Maybe I don't wanna be the bad guy"; Young Children's Resistance to Immoral Actions

text.text: Children are often thought to engage in imagination freely, but research has found they show boundaries in their play.
However, when and how children show limits to moral permissiveness specifically within their pretense is unknown.
We conducted two studies to investigate how and when children display moral boundaries and Imaginative Resistance during imaginative activities.
Study 1 tested 60 children (aged 4-6) with scenarios differing on moral valence (moral or immoral) and agent (self or other) and asked for evaluations of immoral actions in different contexts.
Study 2, a large online replication of study 1 (N = 152; aged 4-7) suggested a developmental trajectory of more Imaginative Resistance with age.
Across both studies, children resisted engagement in immoral play, however, they were more morally permissible in pretend over real contexts.
Thus, Imaginative Resistance follows a developmental trajectory, showing possibilities for malleable moral engagement and intervention opportunities on moral judgements.
Despite the commonly-held belief that imagination is boundless, there are limits to what people can or will imagine, particularly in the moral domain.
Encountering violence, sex, logical fallacies, and feelings of disgust can all trigger a refusal to engage, termed Imaginative Resistance.

Imaginative Resistance occurs when a narrative crosses a held value, boundary, or belief, either moral or non-moral in nature, thus causing an individual to refuse or resist engaging in that situation (Gendler, 2000; Hume, 1757).
text.formatted: Imaginative Resistance occurs when a narrative crosses a held value, boundary, or belief, either moral or non-moral in nature, thus causing an individual to refuse or resist engaging in that situation <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Gendler, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Hume, 1757)</ref>.

text.text: Developmentally, how children engage, or refuse to engage (i.e., resist), with different moral views and frameworks has implications for their general moral development and judgments about ideas, beliefs, or people that may have differing morals.
However, how Imaginative Resistance develops and changes, and if young children display Moral Imaginative Resistance at all remain open questions.
Here, we explore young children's engagement or resistance when introduced to and asked to enact novel, morallydeviant scenarios in the naturalistic, embodied context of pretend play.
How morality develops for children in real world evaluative contexts is a well-studied topic.

Preschool aged children explicitly evaluate moral actions as "good" or "bad" (Wainryb et al., 2004), prefer positive moral behavior, and distinguish between moral and conventional violations (Killen & Smetana, 2015).

text.text: While not at adult levels of moral reasoning, young children are able to make moral judgments and evaluations and begin to consider morality differently depending on context.

Fiction and pretense may serve as a way for children to understand and be exposed to a wide variety of ideas and concepts, including novel moral actions and conventions, similar to how fiction has been viewed as important to moral understanding in adults (i.e., as a "moral laboratory" (Hakemulder, 2000)).

text.text: Pretend play is a prime context to study moral judgements in young children because it is a developmentally appropriate, naturally occurring activity (Weisberg, 2015) containing characters and stories where moral themes can occur or be explored.

text.text: There are two possibilities for how and why children may display Moral Imaginative Resistance in thematically negative play.
One possibility is that Imaginative Resistance may occur as a result of the play itself crossing a value or belief.
For example, a young child may not want to play a game where their doll gets thrown into a volcano as a human sacrifice because they think hurting people is wrong.
However, a second possibility is the role the child takes on within the theme causes Moral Imaginative Resistance.
Children may not want to play the villain in a superhero story, instead wanting to role play a prosocial "good guy" instead.
Imaginative Resistance would not occur if children left their morality behind in the real world but might if children's reality bias in play extends to morals.

Generally, children prefer realism in their pretend play, and for their pretend play to be realistic (Harris, 2021) and three to four-year-olds not only bring real-world knowledge into pretense, but also protest when the pretense goes against their pre-held knowledge (Van de Vondervoort & Friedman, 2017), a form of non-moral Imaginative Resistance.

text.text: Thus, moral violations may present an imaginative boundary to children, driven by the realism of the scenario.
In previous work, four-year-old children judge both immoral and socially impermissible events as impossible, and that their occurrence requires magical involvement (Shtulman & Phillips, 2018).

But, they judge these actions as more permissible in a fantastical context (Fast & Van Reet, 2018), suggesting children may bring moral judgments into pretense.

text.text: Children may also display Imaginative Resistance differently when they engage in pretend play, as opposed to just being presented with scenarios.

Children do show immoral actions and themes in their pretense, and have been observed pretending to kill toys or other children (i.e., Dunn & Hughes, 2001; Galman, 2021; Howe et al., 1998), and cook (i.e., Sturdivant & Alanis, 2021) or steal babies (i.e., Logue & Detour, 2011).

text.text: However, even during these scenarios, children still showed Imaginative Resistance to specific components within the pretense, such as actually portraying or playing the role of the immoral or antagonistic agent (e.g., Logue & Detour, 2011).

text.text: The question of which situations, and which types of actions cause Moral Imaginative Resistance for children in their pretend play is still open.

The current two studies were developed to examine Moral Imaginative Resistance in 4 to 7-year-old children's thematically negative pretend play though their willingness to engage with moral and immoral actions conducted by either the themselves or a moral 'other'.

We hypothesized children would engage in more Moral Imaginative Resistance to playing immoral over moral scenarios within pretense (i.e., they will prefer to play moral scenarios), given that children use an objective moral framework (Heiphetz & Young, 2017; Nichols & Folds-Bennett, 2003) and have a preference for other's moral behavior in pretense (Fast & Van Reet, 2018).

text.text: Further, we hypothesized children will resist pretense scenarios where they have to embody the antisocial or immoral agent more than when others portray the immoral agent.

Finally, we hypothesized a developmental trajectory for Moral Imaginative Resistance, where younger children will display more resistance across both moral valence (moral or immoral) and agent (self or other).
Study 1 consisted of 60 children and their primary caregiver, recruited in the summer of 2023 from parks in a suburban area outside a large east-coast city.
An additional 20 children failed the warm-up task answering questions about pretense and reality and were excluded as we could not be confident in their understanding of pretend actions.
Children were between the ages of 51 and 82 months (Mean = 66.42, SD = 9.01).
There was an uneven distribution of age, with 14 (23.3%) four-year-olds, 30 children (50%) five-yearolds, and 16 (26.7%) six-year-olds.
The child sample was 71.7% female and 28.3% male.
Child race was reported by parents as 45.9% White, 18% Asian, 4.9% Black, 3.3% Hispanic, 3.3% MENA (Middle Eastern and North African), and 11.4% mixed-race or other.
Primary caregivers were between the ages of 28 and 59 (Mean = 37.74, SD = 4.9).

Religiously, this sample was 24.6% Catholic, 19.7% Protestant or other Christian, 9.8% Muslim, 3.3% Agnostic, 3.3% Buddhist, 3.3% Hindu, 1.6% Jewish, 1.6% Atheist, and 22.9% of caregivers said other or chose not to respond.
Children's Imaginative Resistance Children's Imaginative Resistance was measured through a card-sorting task developed for this study.
Each card had an image corresponding to one of 24 pretense scenarios, evenly distributed among morality (moral or immoral) and moral agent (self or other), with six items in each.
Children were asked "would you want to play…" followed by the pretend play scenario and sorted into yes/maybe/no.
As this measure included situations of pretend violence, harm, and death, parents were able to red-line scenarios.
A total play Imaginative Resistance score was calculated as the mean score (yes = -1, maybe = 0, no = 1) across all 24 scenarios.
All items from all measures are available in supplementary materials.
Child Moral Imagination To measure child Moral Imagination, we developed a measure asking the child if it is ever okay to do something traditionally impermissible, such as hitting someone.

Items spanned across five moral domains; fairness/, loyalty/betrayal, authority/subversion, care/harm, and purity/sanctity (Graham et al., 2013), and children were asked whether the action would be ok to do in real life, when pretending, and when joking.

text.text: This measure allowed us to test what domain of moral behaviors children were more likely to resist against, if any.
Children's moral evaluations were measured via a moral transgression task developed by Killen et al. (2011) for use with 4-6-year olds.
text.formatted: Children's moral evaluations were measured via a moral transgression task developed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Killen et al. (2011)</ref> for use with 4-6-year olds.

text.text: Children were asked for the intent of a transgressor (Alex), a justification for that intent, an evaluation of the act, a justification for the evaluation, and, as an open-ended response, the emotions of victim and the transgressor.
The moral evaluation score was the average of intent judgement and evaluation of the act.
We developed a 12-item questionnaire to measure parental reports of child negatively themed play.

Items were chosen from negative themes described in the play therapy literature (i.e., Benedict, 2004; Bruin, 2018; Snow et al., 2007) and reports of themes in studies focused on other topics within play (i.e., Bauman, 2015; Hellendoorn & Harinck, 1997; Sturdivant & Alanis, 2021).

text.text: Recruitment and participation occurred in several local parks in the Mid-Atlantic region of the USA from July to September of 2023.

Parents and children were approached by a researcher, completed consent and assent forms, and then parents complete their questionnaire via QR code while children worked with the researcher individually.
IRB approval was given by Geroge Mason University (Study # 2046296-1).
The researcher defined real and pretend, and presented 4-6 warm up vignettes of real and pretend characters (e.g.
Tinkerbell, Spiderman, President Obama).
Participants were excluded if they got more than one reality judgement incorrect.
Once children passed, they were given the Moral Imaginative Resistance card sort task for all 24 scenarios (unless red-lined by the parent).
Then, children asked if they would actually play one of the "maybe-play" scenarios for a 10-minute free play time.
If there were no cards in the "maybe-play" square, participants were offered one from the "no-play" square.
Children were offered up to three scenarios, and, if no scenario was selected, told to play whatever they liked.
After the free-play session, the researcher asked the child what game and character they played.
Finally, participants were then given the child Moral Imagination task and the child moral evaluation vignettes.
All 60 participants completed the pre-play Moral Imaginative Resistance card sorting task.

Children made judgements about wanting to play due to the moral valence of the pretense scenario and the actions within and not only because they did not like the game as evidenced by interactions such as these during the card sorting task:
Experimenter: "Do you want to play a game where you are a solider sword fighting and the other person pretends to hurt you?"
Participant 014: "No, that's too mean."
And:
Experimenter: "Do you want to play a game where you are a villain and steal all of the townspeople's toys?"
Participant 030 pointing to the 'No' box: "Cause that's too evil."

For preschoolers' displays of Moral Imaginative Resistance in their thematically negative pretense, there was a main effect of moral valence, where children preferred positive moral valence over negative moral valence.
However, there was no effect for how they engaged in that moral or immoral behavior (i.e. as themselves or another agent), and resistance did not differ across age.
Thus, our first hypothesis that Moral Imaginative Resistance would be engaged more often for immoral over moral scenarios was supported.
Young children seemed to incorporate their real world moral values into their pretense, consistent with past literature (Fast & Van Reet, 2018; Kushnir, 2022).

text.text: There was no main effect found for moral agent, though this may be influenced by our small sample size.
However, when enacting the pretense scenarios, the majority of children across pretense scenarios reported playing as the good guy in their pretense and less than a third as the bad guy.
Perhaps who plays the moral agent does not matter when abstractly discussing the pretense scenarios but does when it comes to active, embodied imaginative engagement.
Additionally, we found no age effects for Moral Imaginative Resistance which was surprising, considering morality and moral understanding follow a developmental trajectory.
However, that effect may be due to the relatively small sample size at each age bracket.
Thus, we conducted study two to replicate our findings with a more diverse sample of participants.

The scenarios with the least amount of Imaginative Resistance were pretending to be trapped in a bad flood and someone else trying to help them onto their boat (M = -.47, SD = .77) and pretending to be a firefighter where a house is burning down (M = -.47, SD = .78).

There was no main effect of domain type [Wilk's λ = 0.216, F(4,140) = 1.558, p = 0.216, η² p = 0.11], nor was there an interaction of domain with age [Wilk's λ = 0.615, F(12,436) =0.836, p = 0.608, η² p = 0.017].

Moral evaluations for study 2 were open-ended responses. 103 out of 110 children who responded to this question judged the action of pushing someone off the swing as "not okay" or "not alright", with reasons such as "because that's mean" and "because people might get hurt".
93.5% of participants stated that the child doing the pushing through their actions were wrong and 4.6% responded that the child thought their actions were right.
Study 2 replicated and extended the findings from Study 1.

Similar pretense scenarios invoked the most and least amount of Imaginative Resistance across both studies, and we found age effects with our larger sample size, suggesting Imaginative Resistance may have a developmental trajectory.
For the interaction between agent and morality, it seems that no individual difference is driving the interaction effect, but that the interaction is being driven by main effects.
Further, young children again find moral violations more permissible in a pretend context than in real life or when the offender is joking.

Thus, the introduction of make-believe into a setting may be enough psychological distance for a child to view moral violations as more okay, though moral permissibility differed depending on the child and the violation, suggesting individual differences.

Similar to Study 1, the majority of the moral evaluations for a story containing an act of harm judged the act as immoral, suggesting that, when presented with a realistic scenario, 4-7-year-olds are able to provide moral evaluations.
Children display Imaginative Resistance in response to morally-deviant pretend play scenarios.
Across two studies, we found children were less likely to want to engage in pretense containing immoral versus moral actions, supporting our first hypothesis.
Our second hypothesis, that children will resist pretense scenarios where they are playing the immoral over moral agent was partially supported.

While neither of the current studies showed a main effect of agent on Imaginative Resistance Study 2 showed an interaction between agent and moral valence, where children showed more resistance to the self acting as the immoral agent than others acting as the immoral agent, and less resistance to the self being good than others being good (in an immoral scenario).
This experimentally supports past observational work where, despite immoral themes being present, children did not want to physically be the one enacting those immoral themes (Logue & Detour, 2011).
text.formatted: This experimentally supports past observational work where, despite immoral themes being present, children did not want to physically be the one enacting those immoral themes <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Logue & Detour, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Our third question was where there is a developmental trajectory to moral imaginative resistance.
We initially hypothesized that younger children would display more Moral
Imaginative Resistance, but our Study 2 showed an effect of age in the opposite direction.
Older children displayed more Imaginative Resistance, primarily driven by 4-year-olds displaying less Imaginative Resistance than 6-and 7-year-olds, pointing to a developmental shift around age 5.

Perhaps Imaginative Resistance draws upon similar cognitive underpinnings as possibility judgements (which shift between 4-and 8-years old, Shtulman & Carey, 2007) or relies on developing a firmer idea of the moral self (which begins to emerge around age 5 (Söldner et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Perhaps Imaginative Resistance draws upon similar cognitive underpinnings as possibility judgements (which shift between 4-and 8-years old, Shtulman & Carey, 2007) or relies on developing a firmer idea of the moral self (which begins to emerge around age 5 <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Söldner et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Another possible explanation is the introduction of more formal schooling at this age, containing more explicit instruction of what is considered "proper" or "improper" play and behavior, but more research is required to investigate this shift in moral engagement.
Distance also seemed to affect Moral Imagination and Imaginative Resistance.
In the Moral Imagination task, moral judgements on pretend actions were judged more permissible than joking actions, which were judged more permissible than real ones.

There were no difference across age, perhaps because either the range of ages was too narrow to detect a developmental trajectory, or because the scenarios were all within the age-appropriate range and were not too complicated for the younger participants, resulting in a celling effect.
However, our results suggest moral evaluations and Imaginative Resistance may be context-dependent in children, dependent on how close to reality the immoral scenario is.

A gradient of reality status on moral evaluations on immoral actions may exist, where immoral actions are deemed most permissible in pretend, somewhat permissible when joking, and least permissible in real-life.

These findings are consistent with the past work of fictionality influencing moral evaluations (Sabo & Giner-Sorolla, 2017) and other work in preschoolers where fantastical contexts allow immoral actions to be permissible more than in realistic or real narratives (Fast & Van Reet, 2018) or require fantastical elements to even occur (Shtulman & Phillips, 2018).

text.text: There was no significant effect of moral domain type on the moral judgements across reality context in either study.
This may be because any differences found in the reality context were washed out by the increased Moral Imagination engaged with in the pretend and joking contexts compared to the reality context.

Perhaps domain differences in moral judgments found in realistic or real contexts (e.g., Ball et al., 2017) do not extend to pretend contexts even though general moral judgments can and do (Fast & Van Reet, 2018), though further research is needed.
text.formatted: Perhaps domain differences in moral judgments found in realistic or real contexts (e.g., Ball et al., 2017) do not extend to pretend contexts even though general moral judgments can and do <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Fast & Van Reet, 2018)</ref>, though further research is needed.

text.text: While this Moral Imagination measure spanned moral domains in order to ensure a range of moral contexts for participants to engage with, the primary purpose was to examine Moral Imagination across contexts varying in closeness to reality.

Further studies could be more Young Children's Resistance to Immoral Actions 22 specifically tailored to focus on situations spanning moral domains to see whether or not differences domain-based judgements in this age groups extend to varying contexts.
This study is the first to explore Moral Imaginative Resistance in a developmental context and through embodied engagement.

Taken together, these two studies suggest Moral Imaginative Resistance follows a developmental trajectory, with resistance of morally-deviant behavior increasing with age, but even young children still view immoral actions as more morally permissible in non-realistic contexts.
The flexibility of moral engagement and disengagement supports morality as malleable in early childhood and that moral views may be more expansive with increased psychological distance of reality.
